feedback: If a learner says 'it's all just dirt', point to the separated layers: 'The stones and sand that sank are broken-down rock; the dark floating bits are rotted plants — that's two different things mixed together.'
If a learner denies any link to rock, direct attention to the gritty sand and stones at the bottom: 'Those grains are tiny pieces of rock.'
Praise naming each layer and saying where it came from, not just listing colours.
activities.intendedInsight: Soil is a mixture: it separates into broken-down rock particles (sand/silt/clay) plus decomposed plant matter (humus), so it is not one single substance.
learnerActions: Scoop soil into a clear jar and fill with water, leaving space at the top.
Put the lid on, shake well, then set the jar down and leave it to settle.

Watch and record what settles first, what settles last, and what floats — you will typically see heavy stones and sand sink first, finer silt next, cloudy clay settle slowly on top, and dark bits of rotted leaf (humus) float; write down what you actually observe, as real soils vary.
Draw and label the layers you see, naming which are broken-down rock and which are once-living matter.
Use a hand lens on a pinch of dry soil to spot rock grains and small pieces of plant material up close.
activities.title: Settling jar: watch soil pull apart into its parts

feedback: If a learner says 'all soils are the same', contrast the drainage times they actually measured, for example: 'Look how much faster the water came through the sandy one than the clay one.' (Use the class's real results; dry, cracked clay can sometimes let water through quickly at first.)
If a learner claims one soil is simply best, ask 'best for what?' — clay holds water, sand drains quickly; each suits different conditions.
Reinforce the fair-test idea: 'We used the same amount of soil, the same amount of water, the same-sized funnels and the same timing, so the difference is most likely caused by the type of soil.'
activities.intendedInsight: Different soils have different, testable properties: water drains fast through sandy soil and slowly through clay, and these differences matter for which plants grow well — no single soil is universally 'best'.
learnerActions: Set up three funnels or pots, one with sandy soil, one with clay soil, one with loam, each with the same amount of soil.
Pour the SAME amount of water into each at the same time to make it a fair test.
Watch and time how fast water drains through each, and record which is fastest and slowest.
Feel each soil (with permission) and note whether it is gritty or sticky.
Describe how the soils differ and suggest why a plant might prefer one soil over another.
activities.title: Fair drainage race: sandy vs clay vs loam

feedback: If a learner picks only 'rock' or only 'dead plants' as what soil is made of, remind them it is BOTH mixed together.
If a learner mismatches drainage, link back to the drainage race results.
Note: sorting and matching check recall and classification; they do not by themselves show a learner can run or reason through an investigation — pair them with the hands-on benches.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can classify soils by observable properties and articulate that soil's two core ingredients are broken rock and humus.
learnerActions: Sort soil cards or samples into gritty vs sticky groups.
Match each soil type (sandy, clay, loam) to its drainage speed (fast, slow, in between).
Answer: 'What is soil made of?' choosing the answer that names both broken-down rock and decomposed organic matter.
For plants: discuss why a soil's drainage might help or hinder certain plants.
activities.title: Sort and match soils by property
